anti_overlap: fd-ethology-pair-bond-formation covers behavioral sequencing of bond formation; this covers the mathematical structure of the compatibility model itself
decision_lens: Score calibration — compatibility formulas must produce diverse outcomes across the realistic range of input combinations, not just at extremes
distance_rationale: Matchmaking engineers solve the exact same multi-factor compatibility scoring problem but operate under real-world validation pressure (did these people actually date?) rather than aesthetic preference.
expected_isomorphisms: Driver weight calibration maps directly to feature importance in compatibility models. Asymmetric scoring (A likes B more than B likes A) is standard in recommendation systems and applies directly. Score saturation and decay functions for time-based drivers are well-studied in engagement modeling.
focus: Romantic attraction driver design as a multi-factor compatibility scoring problem — how dating platform engineers balance driver weights, asymmetry, and emergent preference discovery
name: fd-matchmaking-compatibility-weighting
persona: Senior ML engineer at a large-scale matchmaking platform who has designed and A/B-tested compatibility models across millions of user pairs
review_areas: Evaluate whether the 7 driver categories are additive, multiplicative, or threshold-gated — and whether the chosen combination avoids score compression (where all pairs converge toward 0.5)
Check for the 'dominant driver problem': if aesthetic proximity is already the backbone of friendship, it will dominate attraction scoring and make other drivers cosmetic modifiers
Assess whether asymmetric attraction is structurally supported — most real compatibility models must handle A→B scores independently from B→A; the brainstorm flags this as an open question

Evaluate whether 'spark' vs 'gradual accumulation' is a model parameter or an emergent property — platform engineers found that purely accumulative models produce clingy dynamics while threshold-event models create brittle pairing

Check whether the circumstantial/proximity driver creates a recency bias that overwhelms quality signals — elves who happen to share a workshop would always outcompete distant but highly compatible elves
Assess whether the system produces the 'long tail' of unexpected pairings that make simulations feel alive, rather than only matching the obvious top-scoring pairs

severity_examples.condition: No driver hierarchy, no gating logic, additive scoring without normalization
severity_examples.scenario: All 7 drivers feed into a single summed score with equal-ish weights, causing aesthetic proximity (already high between friends) to make friendship a near-prerequisite for romance — elves never develop attraction to strangers or rivals

severity_examples.condition: Time-based drivers lack decay or saturation functions
severity_examples.scenario: Proximity/circumstantial driver accumulates unboundedly — two elves in the same workshop for 500 ticks develop maximum attraction regardless of compatibility, crowding out all other drivers

severity_examples.condition: Attraction computed as a single pairwise score rather than two directed scores
severity_examples.scenario: Attraction is always symmetric — both elves feel exactly the same score — eliminating all unrequited love and one-sided longing from the simulation

source_domain: Dating platform ML and recommendation system engineering
success_hints: A batch of 20 randomly generated elves produces a distribution of attraction scores where the top few pairs are not the same elves who are already best friends. Unrequited cases appear naturally without special-casing.
task_context: The brainstorm defines 7 driver categories for elf romantic attraction and identifies design tensions around legibility, overlap with friendship, and number of active drivers.
